# Introduction {background-color="#1a0a3a"}

## The Promise of Machine Learning

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
> Through careful modeling of the world, we can learn informative patterns
> and make **better predictions and better decisions** about the future.

<br>

::: {.fragment}
**This thesis asks:**

How can ML models be *trained* and *evaluated* so they produce
**better decisions** when allocating limited resources?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
<!-- TODO: replace with a figure or animation -->
:::
:::

::: notes
Open with the broad promise. The key word is "decisions" — not just predictions.
Land on the thesis question early.
:::


## A Concrete Motivating Problem

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**The setting:** A public health authority wants to invest resources
in **opioid-related overdose death prevention** across its territory.

<br>

::: {.fragment}
**The constraint:** Budgets are limited —
interventions can only be deployed in **$K$ locations**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Possible interventions:**

- Naloxone distribution
- Outreach campaigns
- Expanded treatment access (methadone, buprenorphine)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
<!-- TODO: map figure of opioid overdose death rates -->
:::
:::

::: notes
Make the stakes real. These are lives. The K-subset selection framing is key.
:::


## The Decision Problem

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
A **discrete optimization problem:**

$$\max_{S \subseteq \mathcal{L},\, |S| = K} \sum_{\ell \in S} y_\ell$$

where $y_\ell$ = overdose deaths at location $\ell$, and we select
the $K$ locations to intervene.

<br>

::: {.fragment}
**Solved trivially:** pick the $K$ locations with highest $y_\ell$.

But we don't observe $y_\ell$ for the future — we need to **predict** it.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
<!-- TODO: small map or bar chart illustration -->
:::
:::

::: notes
This is the simplest knapsack-style problem. Emphasize that we know the solution structure — top-K ranking — which is what makes the mismatch so stark.
:::

## The Disconnect

{{< video animations/rendered/DisconnectHighlight.mp4 width="100%" >}}

::: notes
This is the key insight of the whole thesis. Let it land. The thought experiment is memorable.
:::


## Why This Matters for Opioid Data

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
Opioid overdose deaths are **rare events** — the distribution is
highly right-skewed.

::: {.fragment}
**Consequence for standard training:**

- Error dominated by the many *low-count* locations
- The *high-count* locations — exactly where allocation matters most —
  are underweighted
:::

::: {.fragment}
A model can achieve low MSE by fitting the zeros well,
while [completely missing the at-risk locations]{.accent-coral}.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
<!-- TODO: histogram of opioid death count distribution -->
:::
:::

::: notes
This motivates why the disconnect is especially bad in this domain.
:::


## The Solution: Decision-Focused Learning

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Core idea:** Train the model to maximize **decision quality**
rather than prediction accuracy.

<br>

::: {.fragment}
This family of methods has been called:

- *Predict-then-Optimize* (PtO / PnO)
- *Decision-Focused Learning* (DFL)
- *End-to-End Learning*
- *Decision-Aware Learning*
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.fragment}
**Intuition:** A model that ranks the
[right locations in the top $K$]{.accent-teal}
is more valuable than one with lower MSE
[but wrong rankings]{.accent-coral}.
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Name the field. Emphasize the papers: Wilder, Elmachtoub, Donti.
:::


## The Gradient Challenge

The decision function is **piecewise constant** with respect to model parameters:

$$\frac{\partial \text{Decision}}{\partial \theta} = 0 \quad \text{almost everywhere}$$

::: {.fragment}
A small change in $\hat{y}$ that does not reorder the top $K$
has **zero effect** on the decision — and zero gradient.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Existing approaches** provide approximate objectives or surrogate gradients:

| Approach | Idea |
|---|---|
| SPO+ (Elmachtoub & Rudin, 2022) | Convex surrogate loss |
| DBB (Pogančić et al., 2020) | Interpolated straight-through gradient |
| NID / Perturbation (Berthet et al., 2020) | Smoothing via noise |
| LODL (Shah et al., 2022) | Learned surrogate loss |
:::

::: notes
Don't dwell — just establish that the gradient problem is known and there are many proposed solutions. This motivates the benchmarking chapter.
:::
